reasons: REJECT on an ungrounded and incorrect classificatory claim about an arsenic mineral, on the highest-risk page of the six. The body states 'Rasaśāstra classes it as an upaviṣa, a minor toxic substance' and the same claim is repeated in cautions as 'classed as an upaviṣa'. It is not in record 35bff9b7-012e-456f-a471-50e7d0e527d3, which says nothing about Manaḥśilā beyond naming it in the wick, and it is contradicted by every source I checked.

Verification: Manaḥśilā is classified under Uparasa varga in Rasaśāstra. easyayurveda's Manashila monograph states flatly 'Manashila is a Uparasa according to Rasashastra', and the Manahshila review literature describes it as 'a mineral drug of Uparasa group'. Upaviṣa is a distinct group of semi-toxic plant drugs (Vatsanabha-adjacent: Ahiphena, Dhattura, Gunja, Karaveera, Langali, Bhallataka and the like) and does not include Manaḥśilā. The grounding entry cites the AYUHOM safety-profile paper for this, but that paper's classification is Uparasa, not Upaviṣa.

This is precisely the failure mode the brief names: a plausible-sounding technical detail added to strengthen a safety argument, sourced to a paper that does not say it. The underlying safety point (an arsenic mineral must not be used unpurified) is true and well-sourced; the classificatory dressing is fabricated. Fix by deleting 'Rasaśāstra classes it as an upaviṣa, a minor toxic substance' from the body and 'classed as an upaviṣa' from the caution, keeping 'realgar, arsenic disulphide, never used unprocessed', which is verified.

Secondary concern, to fix in the same pass: the atiyoga list is attributed wholly to 'Caraka's account', but the Caraka source I fetched gives talushosha, galashosha, daha, deafness, blindness, inability to speak and bleeding disorders, while 'delusion' (moha) and 'loss of consciousness' (murcha) come from the Ashtanga Hridaya Su 21 list. Both halves are real; the single attribution to Caraka is not accurate. Split the attribution.

Secondary concern: 'classical processing requires śodhana, described for this mineral as repeated levigation with ginger juice' reads as the method, whereas the literature gives ardraka svarasa (seven bhavana) as one of several shodhana media, with the AYUHOM study testing four media. Phrase as one described method.

Everything else on this page verified and should be preserved. Ashtanga Hridaya Sutrasthana 21 is confirmed as Dhumapana Vidhim Adhyayam. Caraka Sutrasthana 5 (Matrashiteeya) is confirmed to cover dhumapana at 5/20-24, 5/25, 5/37 and 5/38-39, with Sushruta Chikitsa 40 as a further locus. The three types prayogika/snaihika/vairechanika are confirmed, as is the page's honest flag that the record's Vacā and Pippalī are absent from the prayogika varti and that Manaḥśilā belongs to the vairechanika. The three-puffs-per-nostril discrepancy, the contraindication list including post-virechana and post-basti states, and the particle-size/composition findings (54.18 to 15.55 micron, composition unchanged as arsenic disulphide) all check out. citationVerified true is justified.
No therapeutic claims found, and the supervised framing is otherwise appropriate. This is a one-claim reject, not a rewrite.
ungroundedClaims: Rasaśāstra classes it as an upaviṣa, a minor toxic substance — not in the record; Manaḥśilā is classified under Uparasa varga in Rasaśāstra, and Upaviṣa is a group of plant drugs that does not include it

Suggested fix: delete the clause 'with the procedural material placed in Kalpa Sthāna' from both body and citationNote (or replace with 'with procedure treated elsewhere in the text, which was not checked here'), and cut or ground the śodhana preparation/aftercare generalization. Then republish.

reasons: REJECT on rule 5: a vaidya-only, internally administered procedure written as a complete executable protocol. Publishing an uncorroborated volume for a rectally administered oil on a reference that asks to be cited, run by a manufacturer, is the single highest-consequence unverified number in this batch. The writer has already demonstrated the correct treatment elsewhere in this same batch: the Agnikarma page carries a 'Why this page carries no method' section and deliberately drops the record's '<2 sec per point'. The same discipline was available here and was not applied.

No therapeutic claims, no invented dravyas (all four oils are in common_oils), seasons varṣā and śiśira match the record, and the null adverse_events and red_flags are correctly reported as absence of data.

reasons: REJECT: a classical locus is asserted as fact and was never checked. The page states 'Caraka's own caution, as rendered in translations of the rasāyana chapter, is that three things should not be used in excess of dose or for long duration: pippalī, kṣāra and lavaṇa', and repeats the attribution in cautions ('Caraka's rasāyana chapter names pippalī, along with kṣāra and lavaṇa...') and again in FAQ 3.

I fetched the writer's own cited source, the easyayurveda Vardhamana Pippali page, and it carries the sentence with no locus attached at all: it appears there as a standalone principle with no text, sthāna or chapter named. The 'rasāyana chapter' attribution is the page's own addition, recorded in the grounding list as source 'fetched' against evidence that does not contain it.

Independent search contradicts the attribution: secondary sources place the warning in Caraka's Sūtrasthāna ('Charaka in his Sootra Stana has specified not to use Pippali in excess'), not in the Cikitsāsthāna rasāyana chapter. So the page has not merely over-claimed its source, it has most likely put the verse in the wrong sthāna.

This is load-bearing, not incidental. It is the page's entire argument for why the protocol needs a vaidya, and it appears in the answer line's framing, the body, a caution and an FAQ. A reader or a citing clinician would carry the wrong reference away.

Second ungrounded item: 'Long pepper in quantity is not inert alongside conventional medication' is a pharmacological interaction claim with no record support, no fetched source and no grounding entry.

What is right, and should survive the fix: Caraka Cikitsāsthāna 1.3 is confirmed as the Karaprācitīya Rasāyana Pāda and does contain Vardhamāna Pippalī. The 10/6/3-by-bala schedules rising for ten days and tapering for ten over twenty days are confirmed verbatim, as are the kalka/kaṣāya/cūrṇa forms, śaṣṭika śāli with cow's milk and ghee, and shodhana preceding rasāyana. Refusing to reconcile the record's 1-to-10 nineteen-day schedule with the classical one, and recommending neither, is exactly the right handling.

To pass: either drop the chapter attribution and write 'Caraka warns that pippalī, kṣāra and lavaṇa are not to be used in excess of dose or for long duration', citing the source that actually carries it, or verify the Sūtrasthāna locus against a public translation and cite that. The writer had the disambiguation in hand and published the other reading. On a page whose entire value is precision about what Kāśyapa does and does not specify, a misreport of what the chapter specifies is the exact failure class this audit exists to catch.

Fix is narrow and the page is otherwise publishable: change both occurrences to attribute the eastern direction to the preparation (gold triturated on a clean stone facing east), and re-check the body's first mention, which says 'rubbed with honey and water' while the later paragraph and the sources say water, honey and ghee.

Credit where due, and these should be preserved in the corrected version: the page refuses the record's english field 'Pediatric immunization protocol (puṣya-nakṣatra)', states outright that this is not immunisation and not a substitute for a vaccination schedule, and corrects two demonstrably wrong record assertions (Puṣya as the classical position, and the dravya list as Kāśyapa's own).
